findings.text: Within the first paragraph a newcomer learns what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. The page handles the "what is it" and "why does it matter" questions well.
findings.source: header, first lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The one section that would show Athena's headline features (two models, a verdict, costs) is broken. It is the second thing a newcomer sees, so the main promise goes undemonstrated and the page looks unfinished.
findings.source: Check it on a real job: "The records of job 20261029-073603-7kqv could not be read here, so no models, verdict or costs are shown: no reading record for job 20261029-073603-7kqv."

findings.text: The title and almost all of the page are about firstmate, a different project, and go deep into its internals (exit 75, places-held, pending-close records). A newcomer to Athena has to work out that this is only a sample of Athena's output, and most of the content does not answer their questions.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title> and the sections States of a piece of work, Counters, Transitions, Why it is built this way, Claims and sources

findings.text: The next steps are concrete and in order: prerequisites, clone, install, then a first command with what to expect. The "Next step" link in the header takes the reader straight there.
findings.source: Next steps: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm" ... "./setup.sh" ... "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: A newcomer is not the owner. This link sits in the header with no explanation of what the proposals are, which may confuse a first-time visitor.
findings.source: header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: Several glossary entries say the term is not defined, so the reader is left with only partial meanings. This is honest, but it makes the explanation harder for a stranger to follow.
findings.source: Glossary: "The firstmate source does not define a captain call." / "does not define a durable record" / "does not define an endpoint" / "does not define a heartbeat" / "does not define a wake"

findings.text: This describes Athena's internal folder layout. It does nothing for a newcomer, who has no checkout to look in.
findings.source: About this page: "This page's study id, firstmate-work-handling, is the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."

findings.text: The page does show traceability: every statement links to claim ids, and the claims link to the source lines at the pinned commit. This partly makes up for the missing job evidence.
findings.source: header, second lede: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."
